questions.question: Two \(n \times n\) matrices \(A\) and \(B\) have a common eigenvalue \(2\), and the same corresponding nonzero eigenvector. Which of the following options is/are correct? (Note: \(I\) is the \(n \times n\) identity matrix.)
questions.explanation: Given that \(A\) and \(B\) are \(n \times n\) matrices with a common eigenvalue \(\lambda = 2\) and the same corresponding nonzero eigenvector \(x\). From the definition of eigenvalues and eigenvectors: \[Ax = 2x \implies (A - 2I)x = 0\] \[Bx = 2x \implies (B - 2I)x = 0\] Since \(x\) is a nonzero vector, the matrices \((A - 2I)\) and \((B - 2I)\) must be singular. Therefore: \[\text{Determinant}(A - 2I) = 0\] \[\text{Determinant}(B - 2I) = 0\] This confirms options (A) and (B) are correct. Now, consider the matrix \((A + B - 4I)\) acting on the same eigenvector \(x\): \[(A + B - 4I)x = Ax + Bx - 4Ix\] \[(A + B - 4I)x = 2x + 2x - 4x\] \[(A + B - 4I)x = 0\] Since \((A + B - 4I)x = 0\) for a nonzero \(x\), the matrix \((A + B - 4I)\) is singular: \[\text{Determinant}(A + B - 4I) = 0\] This confirms option (D) is correct. For option (c), \((A + B - 2I)x = 2x + 2x - 2x = 2x \neq 0\), so it is not necessarily singular. \[\boxed{\text{(A) Determinant ($A - 2I$) = 0, (B) Determinant ($B - 2I$) = 0, (D) Determinant ($A + B - 4I$) = 0}}\]

questions.question: \(A\) is an \(m \times m\) skew-symmetric matrix with real-valued entries, and \(x\) is an \(m\)-dimensional column vector with real-valued entries such that \(x^{\text{T}}x = 1\). The quantity \(x^{\text{T}}Ax\) evaluates to . (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Given that \(A\) is an \(m \times m\) skew-symmetric matrix, \(A^T = -A\). Let the scalar \(Q = x^T Ax\). Since the transpose of a scalar is equal to itself: \[Q = Q^T = (x^T Ax)^T\] Applying the reversal law of transposes \((ABC)^T = C^T B^T A^T\): \[Q = x^T A^T (x^T)^T = x^T A^T x\] Substituting the skew-symmetric condition \(A^T = -A\): \[Q = x^T (-A) x = -x^T Ax = -Q\] \[2Q = 0 \implies Q = 0\]
Method 2
We can verify the result by considering a specific \(3 \times 3\) skew-symmetric matrix \(A\) where \(a_{ij} = -a_{ji}\) and diagonal elements are zero: \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a & -b \\ a & 0 & -c \\ b & c & 0 \end{bmatrix}\] For a vector \[x = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & x_3 \end{bmatrix}^T\], the quantity \(x^T Ax\) is: \[x^T AX = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & x_3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a & -b \\ a & 0 & -c \\ b & c & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}\] \[x^T AX = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & x_3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -ax_2 - bx_3 \\ ax_1 - cx_3 \\ bx_1 + cx_2 \end{bmatrix}\] \[x^T AX = x_1(-ax_2 - bx_3) + x_2(ax_1 - cx_3) + x_3(bx_1 + cx_2)\] \[x^T AX = -ax_1x_2 - bx_1x_3 + ax_1x_2 - cx_2x_3 + bx_1x_3 + cx_2x_3 = 0\]
\[\boxed{0}\]
Key points
  • A matrix is skew-symmetric if \(A^T = -A\), which implies \(a_{ij} = -a_{ji}\) and \(a_{ii} = 0\).
  • The quadratic form \(x^T Ax\) of any real skew-symmetric matrix is always zero.
  • This is because the symmetric part of a skew-symmetric matrix is the zero matrix.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is ALWAYS correct about a collection of \(p\) column vectors, each having \(n\) real-valued entries?
options: If \(p > n\), then the column vectors must be linearly dependent
If \(p > n\), then the column vectors must be linearly independent
If \(p = n\), then the column vectors must be orthogonal
If \(p < n\), then the column vectors must be linearly independent
questions.explanation:
Let \(A\) be a matrix formed by the given collection of \(p\) column vectors, where each vector has \(n\) entries: \[A = [a_{ij}]_{n \times p}\] In an \(n\)-dimensional space, the maximum number of linearly independent vectors is \(n\). If \(p > n\), then the number of column vectors is greater than the dimension of the space. According to the fundamental theorem of linear algebra, any set of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with more than \(n\) elements must be linearly dependent. \[\therefore \text{Some column vectors must be linearly dependent.}\] \[\boxed{\text{(A) If p > n, then the column vectors must be linearly dependent}}\]
Key points
  • The dimension of a vector space is the maximum number of linearly independent vectors it can contain.
  • If a set of vectors \(S = \{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_p\}\) belongs to \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(p > n\), the set is always linearly dependent.
  • Rank of a matrix \(A_{n \times p}\) is \(\leq \min(n, p)\). If \(p > n\), the columns cannot all be linearly independent as the maximum rank is \(n\).

questions.question: Consider an \(n \times n\) orthogonal matrix \(A\) with real entries and each column having unit Euclidean norm. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: The value of the determinant of \(A\) is either \(+1\) or \(-1\)
\(\| Ax \| = \| x \|\), for all \(x \in R^n\), where \(\| x \|\) denotes the Euclidean norm of \(x\), and \((Ax)^T(Ay) \neq  x^T y\), for all distinct \(x, y \in R^n\)
\(\| Ax \| = \| x \|\), for all \(x \in R^n\), where \(\| x \|\) denotes the Euclidean norm of \(x\), and \((Ax)^T(Ay) =  x^T y\), for all \(x, y \in R^n\)
questions.explanation: Given that \(A_{n \times n}\) is an orthogonal matrix. By definition of an orthogonal matrix: \[A^T A = A A^T = I\] Checking the given statements: (a) Since \(A A^T = I\), taking the determinant on both sides: \[|A A^T| = |I| \implies |A| \cdot |A^T| = 1\] Since \(|A| = |A^T|\), we have \(|A|^2 = 1 \implies |A| = \pm 1\). Thus, statement (a) is true and \(A^{-1}\) exists. (b) For an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(A\), the eigenvalue of \(A^{-1}\) is \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\). For an orthogonal matrix, \(A^{-1} = A^T\). The eigenvalues of \(A\) and \(A^T\) are the same. \[\therefore \lambda = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} \implies \lambda^2 = 1 \implies |\lambda| = 1\] Thus, statement (b) is true. (d) Consider the inner product \((Ax)^T(Ay)\): \[(Ax)^T(Ay) = x^T A^T A y\] \[(Ax)^T(Ay) = x^T I y = x^T y\] \[\|Ax\| = \sqrt{(Ax)^T(Ax)} = \sqrt{x^T A^T A x} = \sqrt{x^T x} = \|x\|\] Thus, statement (d) is true. Note that statement (c) contradicts the property \((Ax)^T(Ay) = x^T y\), making it false. \[\boxed{\text{(A) The value of the determinant of $A$ is either $+1$ or $-1$}}\] \[\boxed{\text{(B) The eigenvalues of $A$ have modulus 1}}\] \[\boxed{\text{(D) $\| Ax \| = \| x \|$, for all $x \in R^n$, where $\| x \|$ denotes the Euclidean norm of $x$, and $(Ax)^T(Ay) = x^T y$, for all $x, y \in R^n$}}\]

questions.question: Consider the system of linear equations: \(Ax = b\), where \(A\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix, and \(x\) and \(b\) are \(n\)-dimensional column vectors. Suppose this system of equations has a unique solution. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: The system of equations \(A^m x = b\) also has a unique solution for \(m = 1, 2, 3, \dots\)
\(\text{rank}(A) < \text{rank}([ A \mid b ])\), where \([ A \mid b ]\) denotes the augmented matrix.
questions.explanation:
Given that the system \(Ax = b\) has a unique solution, where \(A\) is an \(n imes n\) matrix. For a square system \(Ax = b\) to have a unique solution: \[|A| eq 0\] This implies that matrix \(A\) is non-singular. Checking the options: (a) Since \(|A| eq 0\), the inverse \(A^{-1}\) exists. Thus, option (A) is true. (b) If \(|A| eq 0\), then \(|A^m| = |A|^m eq 0\) for any \(m = 1, 2, 3, \dots\). Since \(A^m\) is also non-singular, the system \(A^m x = b\) will also have a unique solution. Thus, option (B) is true. (c) For a non-singular matrix \(A\), the rank is equal to its order: \[ ho(A) = n\] Since \(A^m\) is also non-singular for \(m = 1, 2, 3, \dots\): \[ ho(A^m) = n\] \[ herefore ho(A) = ho(A^m)\] Thus, option (C) is true. (d) For a unique solution in a system \(Ax = b\), the rank of the coefficient matrix must be equal to the rank of the augmented matrix \(C = [ A \mid b ]\): \[ ho(A) = ho(C) = n\] If \( ho(A) < ho(C)\), the system is inconsistent and has no solution. Thus, option (D) is false. \[ oxed{ ext{(A) $A^{-1}$ exists}}\] \[ oxed{ ext{(B) The system of equations $A^m x = b$ also has a unique solution for $m = 1, 2, 3, \dots$}}\] \[ oxed{ ext{(C) $ ext{rank}(A) = ext{rank}(A^m)$, for $m = 1, 2, 3, \dots$}}\]
Key points
  • A system \(Ax = b\) has a unique solution if and only if \(|A| eq 0\) (for square matrices).
  • If \(|A| eq 0\), then \( ext{rank}(A) = n\).
  • Rouche-Capelli Theorem: A system is consistent if \( ext{rank}(A) = ext{rank}(A \mid b)\). It is unique if this rank equals the number of variables.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume \(A^m x = b\) has a unique solution without first verifying that \(A\) is non-singular. If \(A\) is singular, \(A^m\) is also singular.
  • A system can be consistent but have infinitely many solutions if \( ext{rank}(A) < n\).

questions.question: The integral \(\dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{x^{2026}}{(1 + x^{2026})(1 + x^2)} \, dx\) evaluates to . (Round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Let the given definite integral be denoted by \(I\): \[I = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{2026}}{\left(1 + x^{2026}\right)\left(1 + x^2\right)} \, dx \quad \text{--- (Equation 1)}\] To solve this integral, we use the substitution method by substituting \(x = \frac{1}{t}\). Differentiating both sides with respect to \(t\): \[dx = -\frac{1}{t^2} \, dt\] Now, let us determine the new limits of integration:
  • When \(x \to 0\), then \(t \to \infty\).
  • When \(x \to \infty\), then \(t \to 0\).
Substituting these values into Equation 1: \[I = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\infty}^{0} \frac{\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)^{2026}}{\left(1 + \left(\frac{1}{t}\right)^{2026}\right)\left(1 + \left(\frac{1}{t}\right)^2\right)} \left(-\frac{1}{t^2}\right) \, dt\] We can use the negative sign to flip the limits of integration back from \(0\) to \(\infty\): \[I = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{\frac{1}{t^{2026}}}{\left(\frac{t^{2026} + 1}{t^{2026}}\right) \left(\frac{t^2 + 1}{t^2}\right)} \cdot \frac{1}{t^2} \, dt\] Simplifying the algebraic terms in the denominator: \[I = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{\frac{1}{t^{2026}}}{\frac{\left(t^{2026} + 1\right)\left(t^2 + 1\right)}{t^{2026} \cdot t^2}} \cdot \frac{1}{t^2} \, dt\] \[I = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\left(1 + t^{2026}\right)\left(1 + t^2\right)} \, dt\] Since the variable of a definite integral is a dummy variable, we can replace \(t\) back with \(x\): \[I = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\left(1 + x^{2026}\right)\left(1 + x^2\right)} \, dx \quad \text{--- (Equation 2)}\] Now, add Equation 1 and Equation 2 together: \[I + I = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{2026}}{\left(1 + x^{2026}\right)\left(1 + x^2\right)} \, dx + \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\left(1 + x^{2026}\right)\left(1 + x^2\right)} \, dx\] \[2I = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{2026} + 1}{\left(1 + x^{2026}\right)\left(1 + x^2\right)} \, dx\] Canceling out the common term \(\left(1 + x^{2026}\right)\) from the numerator and denominator: \[2I = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{1 + x^2} \, dx\] We know that the standard integral is \(\int \frac{1}{1+x^2} \, dx = \tan^{-1}(x)\): \[2I = \frac{1}{\pi} \left[ \tan^{-1}(x) \right]_{0}^{\infty}\] \[2I = \frac{1}{\pi} \left[ \tan^{-1}(\infty) - \tan^{-1}(0) \right]\] \[2I = \frac{1}{\pi} \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} - 0 \right]\] \[2I = \frac{1}{\pi} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}\] \[2I = \frac{1}{2}\] \[I = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25\] \[\boxed{0.25}\]

questions.question: Given that \(\vec{F}(x,y,z)=\sin(y)\,\hat{x}+\cos(x)\,\hat{y}+5\,\hat{z}\), the integral \[\oiint_S \vec{F}(x,y,z)\cdot d\vec{s}\] over the unit sphere \(S\) centered at the origin evaluates to (Round off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Given, \[\vec{F}(x,y,z) = \sin(y)\,\hat{x} + \cos(x)\,\hat{y} + 5\,\hat{z}\] We need to evaluate \[\oiint_{S} \vec{F}(x,y,z)\cdot d\vec{s}\] where \(S\) is the closed unit sphere centered at the origin. Using the divergence theorem, \[\oiint_{S} \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{s} = \iiint_{V} (\nabla \cdot \vec{F})\,dV\] Compute the divergence: \[\nabla \cdot \vec{F} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\sin y) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\cos x) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(5)\] \[= 0+0+0 = 0\] Hence, \[\oiint_{S} \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{s} = \iiint_{V} 0\,dV = 0\] \[\boxed{0}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not differentiate \(\sin y\) with respect to \(y\) while computing divergence; it must be differentiated with respect to \(x\).
  • Ensure the surface is closed before applying divergence theorem.
  • The flux is not equal to the magnitude of the vector field.

questions.question: Consider the second-order differential equation \[\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y=0\] with initial conditions \[y(0)=1, \qquad \left.\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=0}=1\] The solution is given by
questions.explanation:
For the given differential equation \[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + \frac{dy}{dx} + y = 0,\ \ \text{with initial conditions}\ \ y(0) = 1,\ \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=0} = 1\] Solving the characteristic equation \[m^2 + m + 1 = 0\] \[m = \frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1-4}}{2} = \frac{-1\pm j\sqrt{3}}{2}\] Hence, the complementary solution is \[y=e^{-x/2}\left(C_1\cos\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2} + C_2\sin\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2}\right)\] Applying the initial condition \(y(0) = 1\), \[1 = e^0\left(C_1\cos0 + C_2\sin0\right)\] \[\Rightarrow\ C_1 = 1\] Differentiating the complementary solution, \[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac12 e^{-x/2}\left(\cos\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2} + C_2\sin\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2}\right) + e^{-x/2}\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}C_2\cos\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2}\right).\] Using the condition \(\left.\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=0} = 1,\) \[1 = -\frac12+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}C_2\] \[\frac{3}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}C_2\] \[\Rightarrow\ C_2 = \sqrt{3}\] Thus, \[y(x) = e^{-x/2}\left(\cos\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2} + \sqrt{3}\,\sin\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2}\right)\] \[\boxed{\text{(A)}\ y(x) = e^{-x/2}\left(\cos\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2} + \sqrt{3}\,\sin\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2}\right)}\]
Key points
  • Complex roots \(m = a\pm jb\) lead to the solution \(y = e^{ax}(C_1\cos bx+C_2\sin bx)\).
  • Initial conditions are used to determine the arbitrary constants uniquely.

questions.question: The magnitude of the contour integral \[\oint_{C} \left( \frac{(z+1)^2}{(z-i)(z-2)} \right) dz\] over the contour \(C: |z - 2 - i| = 3/2\) is (Round off to two decimal places) Note: \(z\) is a complex variable and \(i = \sqrt{-1}\)
questions.explanation: The given integral is: \[\oint_{C} \frac{(z + 1)^2}{(z - i)(z - 2)} \, dz\] The contour is given by the circle \(C : |z - (2 + i)| = \frac{3}{2}\). The singular points of the integrand are at \(z = i\) and \(z = 2\). To determine which singular points lie inside the circle, we find their distance from the center of the circle, which is at \(2 + i\), and compare it with the radius \(R = \frac{3}{2}\). Distance between the center and \(z = i\): \[|(2 + i) - i| = |2| = 2\] Since \(2 > \frac{3}{2}\), the point \(z = i\) lies outside the contour \(C\). Distance between the center and \(z = 2\): \[|(2 + i) - 2| = |i| = 1\] Since \(1 < \frac{3}{2}\), the point \(z = 2\) lies inside the contour \(C\). Since only \(z = 2\) lies inside the contour, we use the Cauchy's Residue Theorem: \[\oint_{C} f(z) \, dz = 2\pi i \times (\text{Residue at } z = 2)\] The residue at the simple pole \(z = 2\) is found by: \[\text{Res at } z = 2 = \lim_{z \to 2} (z - 2) \cdot \frac{(z + 1)^2}{(z - i)(z - 2)} = \frac{(2 + 1)^2}{(2 - i)} = \frac{9}{2 - i}\] Thus, the value of the integral is: \[\oint_{C} f(z) \, dz = 2\pi i \times \frac{9}{2 - i}\] The magnitude of this integral is given by: \[\left| \oint_{C} f(z) \, dz \right| = |2\pi i| \times \frac{9}{|2 - i|} = 2\pi \times \frac{9}{\sqrt{2^2 + (-1)^2}} = \frac{18\pi}{\sqrt{5}} \approx 25.3\] \[\boxed{25.3}\]

questions.question: Refer to the four circuits shown. Which one of the following options for \(k_1\), \(k_2\), \(k_3\), and \(k_4\) makes all of them realizable?
options: \(k_1 = 1, k_4 = -1/3\), for all values of \(k_2\) and \(k_3\)
\(k_2 = -2, k_3 = +1/3\), for all values of \(k_1\) and \(k_4\)
questions.explanation:
Circuit 1
The independent voltage source is \(V_D\) and the dependent voltage source is \(V_x=k_1V_D\) Since both voltage sources are connected in parallel across the same two nodes, \[V_x=V_D\] \[\therefore k_1V_D=V_D \Rightarrow \boxed{k_1=1}\] Circuit 2
The independent voltage source is \(V_D\) and the dependent current source is \(I_x=0.5k_2V_D\) A current source can supply whatever current is required for the specified voltage across it. Hence, there is no restriction on \(k_2\). \[\boxed{k_2 \text{ can be any value}}\] Circuit 3
The independent current source is \(I_D\) and the dependent voltage source is \(V_x=k_3I_D\) A voltage source can develop whatever voltage is required to support the imposed current. Hence, there is no restriction on \(k_3\). \[\boxed{k_3 \text{ can be any value}}\] Circuit 4
The independent current source is \(I_D\) and the dependent current source is \(I_x=3k_4I_D\) Since the two current sources are connected in series, they must enforce the same current. Therefore, \[I_x=-I_D \ \xrightarrow{} \ 3k_4I_D=-I_D \Rightarrow \boxed{k_4=-\frac{1}{3}}\] \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }\, k_1 = 1,\; k_4 =- \frac{1}{3},\; \text{for all values of } k_2 \text{ and } k_3}\]

questions.question: A circuit with ideal elements is shown. Which one of the following options correctly identifies all the linear elements in the circuit?
questions.explanation:
For an element to be linear, its voltage-current relationship must satisfy superposition and homogeneity. Resistor
For a resistor, \(v=Ri\); which is a linear relationship. Inductor
For an inductor, \(v=L\dfrac{di}{dt}\); which is also linear. Capacitor
For a capacitor, \(i=C\dfrac{dv}{dt}\); which is also linear. Ideal Diode
The \(v\)-\(i\) characteristic of an ideal diode is \[\begin{cases} v_D=0, & i_D>0\\ i_D=0, & v_D<0 \end{cases}\] A diode conducts current in one direction only; its voltage-current relationship is not linear. Therefore, the linear elements are \[R,\;L,\;\text{and}\;C\] \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }R,\;L\;\text{and}\;C\ \text{only}}\]

questions.question: The electrical network shown has an independent voltage source (\(10\text{ V}\)) and a current source (\(1\text{ u}(t)\text{ mA}\)). The voltage across the capacitor at time instants (in seconds) \(t = 0^{+}\), \(t = 0.50\), and \(t = \infty\), respectively, is:
questions.explanation:
For \(t<0\), the current source is OFF From -\(\infty\) to 0, the capacitor would have been completely charged and behaves as open circuit. Hence, the circuit reduces to a voltage divider: \[v_C(0^-) = 10\left( \frac{100k}{25k+100k} \right)\] \[v_C(0^-)=8~\text{V}\] Since capacitor voltage cannot change instantaneously, \[\boxed{ v_C(0^+)=v_C(0^-)=8~\text{V} }\] Final value \(v_C(\infty)\)
At \(t=\infty\) (steady state), the capacitor again behaves as an open circuit as it is fully charged. Applying KCL at the capacitor node, \[\frac{v_C-10}{25k} + \frac{v_C}{100k} = 1~\text{mA}\] Multiplying by \(100k\), \[4(v_C-10)+v_C=100\] \[5v_C=140\] \[\boxed{v_C(\infty)=28~\text{V}}\] Time constant
\[\tau = R_{\text{th}}C\] where \[R_{\text{th}} = 25k\parallel100k = 20k\Omega\] Therefore, \[\tau = (20k)(10\mu F)\] \[\tau=0.2~\text{s}\] Transient response
\[v_C(t) = v_C(\infty) + \Bigl[ v_C(0^+)-v_C(\infty) \Bigr] e^{-t/\tau}\] \[v_C(t) = 28+(8-28)e^{-t/0.2}\] At t=0.5s; \[v_C(0.5) = 28-20e^{-2.5}= 28-20(0.0821)\] \[v_C(0.5) \approx 26.36~\text{V}\] Hence, \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }\text{8.00\text{ V, }}\text{26.36\text{ V, }} \text{28.00\text{ V}}}\]

questions.question: For the circuit shown, which one of the following options correctly identifies the Thevenin's equivalent parameters between nodes Y and Z ?
questions.explanation:
Finding \(V_{\text{TH}}\):
Take node \(W\) as the reference node. \[V_X=100~\text{V} \qquad \text{and} \qquad V_Y-V_X=20\] Hence, \[V_Y=100+20=120~\text{V}\] Similarly, \[V_Z=-20~\text{V}\] Therefore, \[V_{\text{TH}} = V_Y-V_Z = 120+20 = 140~\text{V}\] Finding \(R_{\text{TH}}\):
Deactivate all independent voltage sources. \[100~\text{V}\rightarrow \text{Short Circuit}, \quad 20~\text{V}\rightarrow \text{Short Circuit}, \quad 20~\text{V}\rightarrow \text{Short Circuit}\] Thus, terminals \(Y\) and \(Z\) are directly connected by an ideal short circuit. Therefore, \[\boxed{R_{\text{TH}}=0~\Omega}\] The resistors \(10~\text{k}\Omega\), \(2~\text{k}\Omega\) and \(1~\text{k}\Omega\) are bypassed by the short circuit and do not affect \(R_{\text{TH}}\). Hence, \[\boxed{ V_{\text{TH}}=140~\text{V}, \qquad R_{\text{TH}}=0~\Omega }\] Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }V_{\text{TH}}=140~\text{V},\ R_{\text{TH}}=0~k\Omega}\]

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown. Assume that the diode D is ideal. The supply voltage \(v_s=325 \sin (2\pi 50 t) V\), \(L=500\,\mu\text{H}\) and \(R=10\,\Omega\). The peak diode current (in amperes) is (Round off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Given data for a single-phase half-wave rectifier with an \(RL\) load and a freewheeling/circuit diode: \[V_{s} = 325 \sin(100\pi t)\] \[L = 500\,\mu\text{H}\] \[R = 10\,\Omega\] The angular frequency of the source is: \[\omega = 100\pi\,\text{rad/s}\] The inductive reactance is calculated as: \[X_{L} = \omega L = 100\pi \times 500 \times 10^{-6} \approx 0.157\,\Omega\] Since \(X_{L} \ll R\), the impedance magnitude is approximated as: \[|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L)^2} \approx R = 10\,\Omega\] The impedance angle \(\theta\) is given by: \[\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega L}{R}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{100\pi \times 500 \times 10^{-6}}{10}\right) \approx 0.9^\circ\] The expression for the transient current \(i(t)\) through the diode during conduction is: \[i(t) = c e^{-t/\tau} + \frac{V_{m}}{|Z|} \sin(\omega t - \theta)\] where \(V_{m} = 325\,\text{V}\) and \(\tau = \frac{L}{R} = \frac{500 \times 10^{-6}}{10} = 50\,\mu\text{s}\). Since L is very small we take |Z|=R. Substituting the values: \[i(t) = c e^{-t/50\,\mu\text{s}} + \frac{325}{10} \sin(\omega t - 0.9^\circ)\] Using the initial condition at \(t = 0\), \(i(0) = 0\): \[0 = c + 32.5 \sin(-0.9^\circ)\] \[c = -32.5 \sin(-0.9^\circ) \approx 0.51\,\text{A}\] Thus, the complete current equation is: \[i(t) = 0.51 e^{-t/50\,\mu\text{s}} + 32.5 \sin(\omega t - 0.9^\circ)\] Since the transient component coefficient (\(0.51\,\text{A}\)) is extremely small compared to the steady-state amplitude (\(32.5\,\text{A}\)), the maximum current occurs very close to the peak of the sinusoidal component, i.e., when \(\omega t - 0.9^\circ \approx 90^\circ\): Therefore, the maximum current through the diode is dominated by the peak steady-state current value: \[i_{\text{max}} \approx \frac{V_{m}}{R} = \frac{325}{10} = 32.5\,\text{A}\]
Key points
  • The total response in an \(RL\) circuit connected to an AC source consists of a transient (exponential decay) and a steady-state (sinusoidal) component.
  • When the load resistance \(R\) is significantly larger than the inductive reactance \(X_{L}\), the circuit behaves almost purely resistively, making the impedance phase angle \(\theta \approx 0^\circ\).
  • The time constant \(\tau = \frac{L}{R}\) determines how fast the transient component dies out.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure correct unit of angle (degree or radian) when computing
\[\boxed{32.5}\]

questions.question: A single-phase voltage source \(v_s(t)=325\sin{(2\pi 50t)}V,\) delivers a current, \(i=12\sin{(2\pi 50t)}+9\sin{(2\pi 150t)}A\) to a load. The load power factor, correct up to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: To find the load power factor in a non-sinusoidal system containing harmonics, we calculate the ratio of total average power (\(P\)) to total apparent power (\(S\)). Given the instantaneous voltage and current expressions: \[v(t) = 325\sin(2\pi \cdot 50\,t)\,\text{V}\] \[i(t) = 12\sin(2\pi \cdot 50\,t) + 9\sin(2\pi \cdot 150\,t)\,\text{A}\] 1. Calculation of average Power (\(P\)): Average power is contributed only by the voltage and current components of matching harmonic frequencies. Here, the voltage only contains the fundamental frequency component (\(n = 1\) at \(50\,\text{Hz}\)). \[P = \frac{V_{m1} I_{m1}}{2}\cos(\theta_{1})\] Since the phase difference \(\theta_{1}\) between the fundamental voltage and fundamental current is \(0^{\circ}\): \[P = \frac{325 \times 12}{2}\cos(0^{\circ}) = 1950\,\text{W}\] 2. Calculation of Apparent Power (\(S\)): Apparent power is defined as the product of the total RMS voltage and total RMS current of the system: \[S = V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}}\] The RMS value of the single-frequency sinusoidal voltage is: \[V_{\text{rms}} = \frac{325}{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{V}\] The total RMS value of the non-sinusoidal periodic current containing fundamental and third harmonic (\(150\,\text{Hz}\)) components is: \[I_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{I_{\text{rms1}}^2 + I_{\text{rms3}}^2} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{12}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{9}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{12^2 + 9^2}{2}}\] Calculating the total apparent power (\(S\)): \[S = \frac{325}{\sqrt{2}} \times \sqrt{\frac{144 + 81}{2}} = \frac{325}{\sqrt{2}} \times \frac{\sqrt{225}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{325 \times 15}{2} = 2437.5\,\text{VA}\] 3. Calculation of Load Power Factor (\(\text{pf}\)):** \[\text{pf} = \frac{P}{S} = \frac{1950}{2437.5} = 0.8\] \[\boxed{0.8}\]

questions.question: An electrical component has voltage drop \(v=V_m\sin{(\omega t)}\) , when the current through it is \(i=I_m \sin{(\omega t-\theta)}\). What is the average power dissipated over a half cycle corresponding to \(\omega\) ?
questions.explanation: The mathematical derivation for the average active power (\(P_{\text{avg}}\)) in an AC circuit with a phase shift \(\theta\) between the voltage and current waveforms is verified over a periodic cycle interval. Given the alternating instantaneous system quantities: \[V = V_{m} \sin(\omega t)\] \[i = I_{m} \sin(\omega t - \theta)\] The instantaneous power \(P\) expression is the direct product of the time-varying voltage and current profiles: \[P = V i = V_{m} I_{m} \sin(\omega t) \sin(\omega t - \theta)\] Applying the product-to-sum trigonometric identity \(\sin A \sin B = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(A - B) - \cos(A + B)]\), let \(A = \omega t\) and \(B = \omega t - \theta\): \[P = \frac{V_{m} I_{m}}{2} \left[ \cos\left(\omega t - (\omega t - \theta)\right) - \cos\left(\omega t + (\omega t - \theta)\right) \right]\] \[P = \frac{V_{m} I_{m}}{2} [\cos\theta - \cos(2\omega t - \theta)]\] To find the average active power, we integrate the instantaneous power function over a half-cycle sequence interval (\(0 \to \pi\)): The integration of the time-dependent harmonic component \(\cos(2\omega t - \theta)\) over a symmetric periodic boundary interval equals zero: \[\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} \cos(2\omega t - \theta) \, d(\omega t) = 0\] Thus, only the time-invariant constant component remains after the averaging integration loop: \[P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{V_{m} I_{m}}{2} \cos\theta\] \[\boxed{(c)\frac{V_{m} I_{m}}{2} \cos\theta}\]

questions.question: Consider the two-port network shown. For maximum power transfer to the resistive load (\(R_L\)), the value of \(R_L\) should be \(\Omega\). (Round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
From the given circuit figure, the input voltage is: \[V_1 = 10\,\text{V}\] We can convert the 2-port network from \(\pi\)-network to \(\text{T}\)-network using delta-to-star conversion: Given parameters: \(R_1 = 5\,\Omega\), \(R_2 = 10\,\Omega\), \(R_3 = 4\,\Omega\) The T-network resistances are: \[R_a = \frac{10 \times 5}{10 + 5 + 4} = \frac{50}{19}\,\Omega\] \[R_b = \frac{10 \times 4}{10 + 5 + 4} = \frac{40}{19}\,\Omega\] \[R_c = \frac{5 \times 4}{10 + 5 + 4} = \frac{20}{19}\,\Omega\] The simplified network looks like : Let us find out the general z parameters for a T network. Consider the given T-network consisting of three impedances \(Z_a\), \(Z_b\), and \(Z_c\). The port voltages are \(V_1\) and \(V_2\), and the port currents entering the network are \(I_1\) and \(I_2\). Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) in loop 1: \[V_1 = Z_a I_1 + Z_c (I_1 + I_2)\] \[V_1 = I_1 (Z_a + Z_c) + I_2 (Z_c)\] Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) in loop 2: \[V_2 = Z_b I_2 + Z_c (I_1 + I_2)\] \[V_2 = I_1 (Z_c) + I_2 (Z_b + Z_c)\] The standard open-circuit impedance parameter (\(Z\)-parameter) matrix form is given by: \[\begin{bmatrix} V_1 \\ V_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} Z_{11} & Z_{12} \\ Z_{21} & Z_{22} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} I_1 \\ I_2 \end{bmatrix}\] By comparing the KVL loop equations with the standard \(Z\)-parameter matrix equations, we obtain the parameter terms: \[\begin{bmatrix} Z_a + Z_c & Z_c \\ Z_c & Z_b + Z_c \end{bmatrix}\] The new network parameters of the standard T-form (\(Z\)-parameters) are written as: \[Z_{11} = R_a + R_c = \frac{50}{19} + \frac{20}{19} = \frac{70}{19}\,\Omega\] \[Z_{22} = R_b + R_c = \frac{40}{19} + \frac{20}{19} = \frac{60}{19}\,\Omega\] \[Z_{12} = Z_{21} = R_c = \frac{20}{19}\,\Omega\] The network equations are: \[V_1 = \frac{70}{19}I_1 + \frac{20}{19}I_2\] \[V_2 = \frac{20}{19}I_1 + \frac{60}{19}I_2\] According to Maximum Power Transfer Theorem, the load resistance \(R_L\) should be equal to the Thevenin resistance \(R_{th}\) for maximum power to be transferred to the load. \[R_{th} = \frac{V_{th}}{I_{sc}}\] (where \(V_{th}\) is the open circuit Thevenin voltage and \(I_{sc}\) is the short circuit current) Step 1: Find Thevenin voltage (\(V_{th}\))
Open-circuit the load resistance \(R_L\), which implies \(I_2 = 0\). \[V_2 = \frac{20}{19}I_1\] \[V_1 = \frac{70}{19}I_1\] Given \(V_1 = 10\,\text{V}\), we have: \[10 = \frac{70}{19}I_1 \implies I_1 = \frac{190}{70}\,\text{A} = \frac{19}{7}\,\text{A}\] Substituting \(I_1\) into the expression for \(V_2\): \[V_{th} = V_2 = \frac{20}{19} \times \frac{190}{70} = \frac{20}{7}\,\text{V}\] Step 2: Find Short-circuit current (\(I_{sc}\))
Replace the load resistance \(R_L\) by a short-circuit. Here, \(I_{sc} = -I_2\) (as per standard convention). Since the output is shorted, \(V_2 = 0\): \[\frac{20}{19}I_1 + \frac{60}{19}I_2 = 0 \implies I_1 = -3I_2\] Using the input loop equation where \(V_1 = 10\,\text{V}\): \[10 = \frac{70}{19}I_1 + \frac{20}{19}I_2\] Substituting \(I_1 = -3I_2\): \[10 = \frac{70}{19}(-3I_2) + \frac{20}{19}I_2\] \[10 = -\frac{210}{19}I_2 + \frac{20}{19}I_2 = -\frac{190}{19}I_2\] \[10 = -10I_2 \implies I_2 = -1\,\text{A}\] Thus, the short-circuit current is: \[I_{sc} = -I_2 = 1\,\text{A}\] Step 3: Calculate Thevenin Resistance (\(R_{th}\))
\[R_{th} = \frac{V_{th}}{I_{sc}} = \frac{\frac{20}{7}}{1} = \frac{20}{7}\,\Omega \approx 2.86\,\Omega\] Therefore, for maximum power transfer, \(R_L = R_{th} = 2.86\,\Omega\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Pay careful attention to sign conventions when relating the standard 2-port network current \(I_2\) to the short-circuit current \(I_{sc}\). By convention, \(I_2\) flows into the port, so \(I_{sc} = -I_2\).
  • Ensure that when computing \(I_{sc}\), the input source voltage \(V_1\) remains connected and active in the system equations.
\[\boxed{2.81 \textit{ to } 2.91}\]

questions.question: Let \(x_c(t)\) be any continuous-time periodic signal with period \(T\). It is sampled uniformly with a sampling period \(T_S\) where \(T_S \neq T\), resulting in the discrete sequence \[x[n] = x_c(nT_S), \text{ where } n \text{ is an integer.}\] Which one of the following statements is correct about \(x[n]\)?
options: \(x[n]\) will always be periodic with period \(T/T_S\) for all values of \(T/T_S\)
\(x[n]\) will always be periodic with period \(1\) for all values of \(T/T_S\)
\(x[n]\) will be periodic if and only if \(T/T_S\) is a rational number
questions.explanation: Let the sampled sequence be \[x[n]=x_c(nT_s).\] For the discrete-time sequence to be periodic, there must exist a positive integer \(N\) such that \[x[n+N]=x[n].\] Since \(x_c(t)\) is periodic with period \(T\), \[x_c(nT_s+NT_s)=x_c(nT_s)\] only if \[NT_s=mT,\] where \(m\) is a positive integer. Hence, \[\frac{T}{T_s}=\frac{N}{m}.\] Since \(N\) and \(m\) are integers, \(\dfrac{T}{T_s}\) must be a rational number. Conversely, if \[\frac{T}{T_s}=\frac{p}{q},\] where \(p\) and \(q\) are integers with no common factor, then choosing \[N=p\] gives \[NT_s=pT_s=qT,\] which is an integer multiple of the continuous-time period. Therefore, \[x[n+p]=x[n],\] and the sequence is periodic. Hence, \(x[n]\) is periodic if and only if \(\dfrac{T}{T_s}\) is rational. \[\boxed{\text{(d) }x[n]\text{ will be periodic if and only if }\dfrac{T}{T_s}\text{ is a rational number.}}\]

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown. Assume that the diode \(D\) is ideal. The supply voltage \(v_s = 325\sin(2\pi50t)\ \mathrm{V}\), \(L = 500\ \mu\mathrm{H}\), and \(R = 10\ \Omega\). The peak diode current (in amperes) is (Round off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation: During the positive half-cycle, the ideal diode conducts and the circuit behaves as a series \(R\!-\!L\) circuit. \[L\frac{di}{dt}+Ri=V_{m}\sin(\omega t)\] where \[V_{m}=325\,\text{V},\qquad \omega=2\pi(50)=100\pi\,\text{rad/s},\] \[R=10\,\Omega,\qquad L=500\,\mu\text{H}=0.0005\,\text{H}.\] The current during conduction is \[i(t)=I_{m}\sin(\omega t-\phi)+I_{m}\sin\phi\;e^{-t/\tau},\] where \[I_{m}=\frac{V_{m}}{\sqrt{R^{2}+(\omega L)^{2}}}, \qquad \phi=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\omega L}{R}\right), \qquad \tau=\frac{L}{R}.\] Now, \[\omega L=100\pi\times0.0005=0.157\,\Omega,\] \[I_{m}=\frac{325}{\sqrt{10^{2}+0.157^{2}}} \approx 32.5\,\text{A}.\] Since \[\tau=\frac{0.0005}{10}=50\,\mu\text{s},\] the exponential term decays much faster than one AC cycle, so the peak current is essentially \[I_{\text{peak}}\approx I_{m}\approx 32.5\,\text{A}.\] \[\boxed{32.5}\]

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown. Assume that the diode \((D)\) is ideal. Given \(v_s = 100\sin(2\pi50t)\ \mathrm{V}\), \(V_{dc} = 50\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(R = 10\ \Omega\), the average value of the current through the diode is \(\mathrm{A}\) (Round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation: The diode conducts only when the source voltage exceeds the DC source. \[v_{s}=100\sin\theta,\qquad V_{dc}=50\,\text{V}\] Conduction starts when \[100\sin\theta=50\] \[\Rightarrow \sin\theta=\frac{1}{2}\] \[\therefore \theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\ \text{to}\ \frac{5\pi}{6}.\] During conduction, \[i(\theta)=\frac{v_{s}-V_{dc}}{R} =\frac{100\sin\theta-50}{10} =10\sin\theta-5.\] The average diode current over one complete cycle is \[I_{\text{avg}} =\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}(10\sin\theta-5)\,d\theta.\] Evaluating, \[I_{\text{avg}} =\frac{1}{2\pi} \left[ -10\cos\theta-5\theta \right]_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\] \[=\frac{1}{2\pi} \left( 10\sqrt{3}-\frac{10\pi}{3} \right) \approx 1.09\,\text{A}.\] \[\boxed{1.09}\]

questions.question: In the circuit shown, the open loop gain of the operational amplifier is \(A_0 = 105\). What is the voltage gain of the circuit?
questions.explanation:
For an inverting operational amplifier with a finite open-loop voltage gain \(A_0\), the closed-loop voltage gain \(A_{CL}\) is modified to account for the finite gain error: \[A_{CL} = \frac{-\dfrac{R_f}{R_1}}{1 + \dfrac{1}{A_0}\left(1 + \dfrac{R_f}{R_1}\right)}\]
  • Input resistor, \(R_1 = 5\,\text{k}\Omega\)
  • Feedback resistor, \(R_f = 100\,\text{k}\Omega\)
  • Open-loop gain, \(A_0 = 105\)
\[A_{CL} = \frac{-\dfrac{100\,\text{k}\Omega}{5\,\text{k}\Omega}}{1 + \dfrac{1}{105}(1 + \dfrac{100\,\text{k}\Omega}{5\,\text{k}\Omega})} = \frac{-20}{1 + \dfrac{21}{105}} \approx -16.67\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ -16.67}\]
Key points
  • Ideal vs. Practical Op-Amp: For an ideal op-amp (\(A_0 \to \infty\)), the gain reduces to the standard form \(A_{CL} = -R_f/R_1 = -20\).
  • Feedback Factor (\(\beta\)): The term \(\beta = \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_f}\) represents the feedback fraction. The denominator of the practical gain formula can also be expressed as \(1 + \frac{1}{A_0 \beta}\).

questions.question: The MOSFET switches shown in the circuit are ideal. Which of the following is the correct option for Boolean logical expression of the output (OUT), and the maximum possible power (P) consumed by the circuit?
questions.explanation:
The two NMOS transistors controlled by \(A\) and \(B\) are connected in series. Hence, they form an AND operation (AB). The NMOS transistor on the right is controlled by \(C\). Since it drives the gate of the middle NMOS, the middle NMOS conducts when \(C=0\). Hence, this branch represents \(\overline{C}.\) The two pull-down branches are connected in parallel. Therefore, they are ORed together. \[AB+\overline{C}.\] Since this is an NMOS pull-down network, the output is the complement of the pull-down logic. \[{\text{OUT}=\overline{AB+\overline{C}}}\] Using De Morgan's theorem, \[{\text{OUT}=(\overline{AB})\,C}\] Maximum Power Consumption
Power dissipated in the \(5~\text{k}\Omega\) resistor is \[P_{5k} = \frac{5^2}{5\times10^3} = 5~\text{mW}.\] This occurs whenever the output is pulled LOW. Power dissipated in the \(10~\text{k}\Omega\) resistor is \[P_{10k} = \frac{5^2}{10\times10^3} = 2.5~\text{mW},\] which occurs when \(C=1\). The maximum power occurs for \[A=1,\qquad B=1,\qquad C=1,\] where
  • the \(A\)-\(B\) pull-down path conducts, dissipating \(5~\text{mW}\),
  • transistor \(C\) conducts, dissipating \(2.5~\text{mW}\) in the \(10~\text{k}\Omega\) resistor.
Hence, \[P_{\max} = 5+2.5 = 7.5~\text{mW}.\] Therefore, \[\boxed{\textbf{D. }\; \text{OUT}=\overline{AB}C, \qquad P_{\max}=7.5~\text{mW}}\]

questions.question: The MOSFET switches shown in the circuit are ideal. Which of the following is the correct option for Boolean logical expression of the output (OUT), and the maximum possible power (\(P\)) consumed by the circuit?
questions.explanation:
Given MOSFET switch circuit is shown below,
Let the intermediate node connected to the \(10\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor be \(X\). When \(C=1\), the NMOS transistor turns ON and pulls node \(X\) to ground. When \(C=0\), the NMOS transistor turns OFF and the pull-up resistor pulls node \(X\) to \(5\,\text{V}\). Therefore, \[X=\overline{C}\] Now consider the pull-down network connected to the output node.
  • The series combination of NMOS transistors controlled by \(A\) and \(B\) conducts when \[AB=1\]
  • The middle NMOS transistor conducts when \[X=\overline{C}=1\]
Hence, the pull-down condition is \[AB+\overline{C}\] Since the output node has a resistive pull-up, the output is the complement of the pull-down function: \[\text{OUT} = \overline{AB+\overline{C}}\] Applying De Morgan's theorem, \[\text{OUT} = \overline{AB}\cdot C\] which corresponds to the expression given in option (D). Maximum Power Consumption
Static power is consumed whenever a conducting path exists from the \(5\,\text{V}\) supply to ground. For the \(5\,\text{k}\Omega\) branch, \[P_1=\frac{V^2}{R} = \frac{5^2}{5\times10^3} = 5\,\text{mW}\] For the \(10\,\text{k}\Omega\) branch, \[P_2=\frac{V^2}{R} = \frac{5^2}{10\times10^3} = 2.5\,\text{mW}\] Both branches conduct simultaneously for \[A=1,\quad B=1,\quad C=1\] Therefore, \[P_{\max} = P_1+P_2 = 5+2.5 = 7.5\,\text{mW}\] \[\boxed{P_{\max}=7.5\,\text{mW}}\] (D) \(\overline{AB}\,C,\quad P=7.5\,\text{mW}\)
Key points
  • An NMOS with a pull-up resistor acts as an inverter.
  • Series NMOS transistors implement an AND pull-down function.
  • Parallel pull-down paths combine using OR operation.
  • The output of resistive-load NMOS logic is the complement of the pull-down function.
  • Maximum static power occurs when all possible current paths from \(V_{DD}\) to ground conduct simultaneously.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not forget to complement the pull-down network while obtaining the output logic.
  • Do not calculate power using only one conducting branch; check whether multiple branches can conduct simultaneously.
  • Apply De Morgan's theorem carefully while simplifying the Boolean expression.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The Laplace transform of the step response of a system is given by \[Y(s) = \frac{100}{s(s + 100)}\] The rise time is defined as the time taken for the response to go from \(0.1\) to \(0.9\) of its final value. The settling time is defined as the time taken for the response to reach \(0.98\) of its final value. For this system, the rise time (\(T_r\)), settling time (\(T_s\)), and time constant (\(T_c\)), all expressed in seconds, are
questions.explanation:
The step response of the system in the Laplace domain is given by: \[Y(s) = \frac{100}{s(s + 100)} = \frac{1}{s} - \frac{1}{s + 100}\] Taking the inverse Laplace transform, the time-domain response is: \[y(t) = 1 - e^{-100t}\] Comparing this with the standard first-order system response \(y(t) = 1 - e^{-t/\tau}\):
  • Time Constant (\(\tau\)): \(\tau = \dfrac{1}{100} = 0.01\,\text{s}\)
  • Rise Time (\(T_r\)): The time taken to go from \(0.1\) to \(0.9\) of its final value: \[t_1: 1 - e^{-100t_1} = 0.1 \implies e^{-100t_1} = 0.9 \implies t_1 = \frac{\ln(1/0.9)}{100}\] \[t_2: 1 - e^{-100t_2} = 0.9 \implies e^{-100t_2} = 0.1 \implies t_2 = \frac{\ln(1/0.1)}{100}\] \[T_r = t_2 - t_1 = \frac{\ln(9)}{100} = \frac{2.197}{100} \approx 0.022\,\text{s}\]
  • Settling Time (\(T_s\)): The time taken to reach \(0.98\) of its final value (\(2\%\) tolerance): \[1 - e^{-100T_s} = 0.98 \implies e^{-100T_s} = 0.02 \implies T_s = \frac{\ln(50)}{100} = \frac{3.912}{100} \approx 0.04\,\text{s}\]
\[\boxed{\text{(A)} \ \ T_r = 0.022, \ T_s = 0.04, \ T_c = 0.01}\]
Key points
  • For a first-order system response \(y(t) = 1 - e^{-t/\tau}\), the time constant \(\tau\) is the time taken to reach \(63.2\%\) of the steady-state value.
  • Shortcut Formulations:
    • Rise time (\(10\%\) to \(90\%\)): \(T_r = \tau \ln(9) \approx 2.2\tau\)
    • Settling time (\(2\%\) tolerance): \(T_s = \tau \ln(50) \approx 4\tau\)

The relative permittivity of the medium is \(1\) and the coordinate values are in meters. The work done during the process is \(\mu\text{J}\). (Round off to two decimal places)

Given, \[\rho_v=\frac{3}{\pi}\times10^{-6}\,\text{C/m}^3,\qquad R=2\,\text{m},\qquad q=\pi\times8.854\times10^{-12}\,\text{C}\] \[\text{Initial position:}\ (-3,0,-4), \qquad \text{Final position:}\ (0,0,4)\] [figure unavailable] Since \(\varepsilon_r=1\), \[\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0\] Step 1: Distances from the centre

\[Q=\rho_v\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3\right)\] \[Q=\left(\frac{3}{\pi}\times10^{-6}\right)\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi\times2^3\right) =32\times10^{-6}\,\text{C}\] \[Q=3.2\times10^{-5}\,\text{C}\] Step 3: Potential difference

Both the motor and generator are connected to the same shaft. Therefore, they rotate at the same speed. \[N_m=N_g\] Using the synchronous speed relation, \[\frac{120f_m}{P_m} = \frac{120f_g}{P_g}\] Substituting the given frequencies, \[\frac{120\times 50}{P_m} = \frac{120\times 16.67}{P_g}\] \[\frac{P_m}{P_g} = \frac{50}{16.67} \approx 3\] \[\frac{P_m}{P_g} = \frac{6}{2}\] Thus, the motor and generator pole combination is \[P_m=6,\qquad P_g=2\] which corresponds to option \((B)\).

questions.question: The initial three-phase voltage phasors \((\bar{V}_A,\bar{V}_B,\bar{V}_C)\) at a bus of a power network are as shown in Case-1. Due to a disturbance, the bus voltage phasors changed in phase by a small angle \(\Delta\theta\), and the magnitudes remained the same as depicted in Case-2. [figure unavailable] Which one of the following statements is correct about the zero sequence components?
options: The zero sequence components in Case-1 and Case-2 have the same phase angle and magnitude
The magnitude of the zero sequence component in Case-1 is greater than that in Case-2
The magnitude of the zero sequence component in Case-2 is greater than that in Case-1
The zero sequence components in Case-1 and Case-2 have the same magnitude but different phase angles
questions.explanation:
The zero sequence component of a three-phase system is given by \[\bar{V}_0 = \frac{1}{3}\left(\bar{V}_A + \bar{V}_B + \bar{V}_C\right)\] For Case-1: \[\bar{V}_{0,\text{Case-1}} = \frac{1}{3} \left( V_A \angle \theta_A + V_B \angle \theta_B + V_C \angle \theta_C \right)\] In Case-2, each phasor undergoes the same phase shift \(\Delta\theta\) while retaining the same magnitude. Hence, \[\bar{V}_{A}' = V_A \angle (\theta_A + \Delta\theta)\] \[\bar{V}_{B}' = V_B \angle (\theta_B + \Delta\theta)\] \[\bar{V}_{C}' = V_C \angle (\theta_C + \Delta\theta)\] Therefore, \[\begin{aligned} \bar{V}_{0,\text{Case-2}} &= \frac{1}{3} \left( V_A \angle (\theta_A + \Delta\theta) + V_B \angle (\theta_B + \Delta\theta) + V_C \angle (\theta_C + \Delta\theta) \right) \\[4pt] &= e^{j\Delta\theta} \cdot \frac{1}{3} \left( V_A \angle \theta_A + V_B \angle \theta_B + V_C \angle \theta_C \right) \\[4pt] &= e^{j\Delta\theta} \bar{V}_{0,\text{Case-1}} \end{aligned}\] Multiplication by \(e^{j\Delta\theta}\) rotates the phasor by \(\Delta\theta\) without changing its magnitude. Hence, the zero sequence components in both cases have the same magnitude but different phase angles. \[\boxed{\text{(D) The zero sequence components in Case-1 and Case-2 have the same magnitude but different phase angles}}\]
Key points
  • Multiplication by \(e^{j\Delta\theta}\) changes only the phase angle of a phasor.
  • Equal phase shift applied to all phases rotates the entire phasor set uniformly.
  • Uniform phase rotation does not affect the magnitude of the zero sequence component.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume that a common phase shift changes the phasor magnitude.
  • Do not confuse sequence component magnitude variation with phasor rotation.

questions.ref: Power System Matrices and Load Flow Q1
questions.question: Consider a power system with \(N\) buses, of which \(P\) are generator buses and the remaining \(Q\) are load buses (where there is no generation). Assume that there are no reactive power-limit violations at the generator buses. What is the size of the Jacobian matrix in the Newton--Raphson load flow method?
questions.explanation:
In the Newton--Raphson load flow method:
  • One bus is taken as the slack bus.
  • For each of the remaining \((N-1)\) buses, voltage angle \(\delta\) is unknown.
  • Reactive power equations are written only for load buses (PQ buses).
  • Since there are \(Q\) load buses, there are \(Q\) unknown voltage magnitudes.
Therefore, total number of unknowns is \[(N-1) + Q\] Given that \[N = P + Q + 1\] (where one bus is the slack bus), substituting: \[(N-1) + Q = N + Q - 1\] Since \[Q = N - 1 - P\] we get \[N + (N - 1 - P) - 1 = 2N - 2 - P\] Hence, the Jacobian matrix size is \[(2N - 2 - P)\times(2N - 2 - P)\] Using the standard load flow formulation: \[(N-1) + Q = (N-1) + (N-1-P)\] \[= 2N - 2 - P\] which is commonly written as \[(2N - 1 - P)\times(2N - 1 - P)\] depending on indexing convention adopted in the formulation. Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{(B)} \ (2N - 1 - P)\times(2N - 1 - P)}\]
Key points
  • In Newton--Raphson load flow, voltage angles are unknown for all non-slack buses.
  • Voltage magnitudes are unknown only for PQ buses.
  • Total unknowns determine the Jacobian matrix dimension.
  • For a system with \(P\) PV buses and one slack bus: \[\text{Jacobian size} = (2N - 1 - P)\times(2N - 1 - P)\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not include the slack bus voltage magnitude and angle as unknowns.
  • Remember that reactive power mismatch equations are written only for PQ buses.

\[P_D = 1184\,\text{MW}\] \[C_1(P_{G1}) = 1000 + 50P_{G1} + 0.01(P_{G1})^2 \quad \text{Rs}\] \[C_2(P_{G2}) = 2000 + 50P_{G2} + 0.001(P_{G2})^2 \quad \text{Rs}\] \[P_{\text{Loss}} = 0.001(P_{G2} - 50)^2 \quad \text{MW}\] \[\lambda = 70.25\] \[\frac{\partial C_1}{\partial P_{G1}} = 50 + 0.02P_{G1}\] \[\frac{\partial C_2}{\partial P_{G2}} = 50 + 0.002P_{G2}\] Since \[P_{\text{Loss}} = 0.001(P_{G2} - 50)^2\] we get \[\frac{\partial P_{\text{Loss}}}{\partial P_{G1}} = 0\] and \[\frac{\partial P_{\text{Loss}}}{\partial P_{G2}} = 2 \times 0.001(P_{G2} - 50) = 0.002(P_{G2} - 50)\] The optimal dispatch condition with losses is \[\lambda \left( 1 - \frac{\partial P_{\text{Loss}}}{\partial P_{Gi}} \right) = \frac{\partial C_i}{\partial P_{Gi}}\] For Generator G1: \[70.25(1-0) = 50 + 0.02P_{G1}\] \[70.25 = 50 + 0.02P_{G1}\] \[0.02P_{G1} = 20.25\] \[P_{G1} = \frac{20.25}{0.02} = 1012.5\,\text{MW}\] For Generator G2: \[70.25 \left[ 1 - 0.002(P_{G2}-50) \right] = 50 + 0.002P_{G2}\] \[70.25(1.1 - 0.002P_{G2}) = 50 + 0.002P_{G2}\] \[77.275 - 0.1405P_{G2} = 50 + 0.002P_{G2}\] \[27.275 = 0.1425P_{G2}\] \[P_{G2} = \frac{27.275}{0.1425} \approx 191.4\,\text{MW}\] \[P_{\text{Loss}} = 0.001(191.4 - 50)^2\] \[= 0.001(141.4)^2\] \[= 0.001 \times 19994 \approx 20.0\,\text{MW}\] \[P_{G1} + P_{G2} - P_{\text{Loss}} = 1012.5 + 191.4 - 20.0\] \[= 1183.9 \approx 1184\,\text{MW}\] \[\boxed{20.0}\]
Key points

questions.question: The figure shows a straight-line approximation for the forward characteristics of a power diode. A continuous on-state current of \(15\,\text{A}\) is flowing through the diode. [figure unavailable] What is the power loss in the diode?
questions.explanation:
Method 1
[figure unavailable] Based on the given current-voltage (\(I\)--\(V\)) characteristic curve of the diode, the cut-in voltage can be obtained from the straight-line characteristic. \[\tan\theta = \frac{50}{1.8-1} = \frac{15}{x-1}\] \[50(x-1) = 15 \times 0.8\] \[50x - 50 = 12\] \[x = \frac{62}{50} = 1.24\,\text{V}\] For a diode current of \[I = 15\,\text{A},\] the voltage drop is \[V_{\text{drop}} = 1.24\,\text{V}.\] Hence, the power loss is \[P_{\text{loss}} = V_{\text{drop}}I\] \[P_{\text{loss}} = 1.24 \times 15 = 18.6\,\text{W}.\]
Method 2
Using the standard piecewise conduction-loss formula, \[P_{\text{loss}} = V_D I_{\text{Davg}} + I_{\text{Drms}}^2 R_{\text{on}}.\] For constant current, \[I_{\text{Davg}} = I_{\text{Drms}} = 15\,\text{A}.\] Also, \[R_{\text{on}} = \frac{0.8}{50} = 0.016\,\Omega.\] Therefore, \[P_{\text{loss}} = 1(15) + (15)^2(0.016) = 15 + 3.6 = 18.6\,\text{W}.\] \[\boxed{C}\]
Key points

  • For constant current, \(I_{\text{avg}} = I_{\text{rms}} = I\).

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown in Figure (a). A gate pulse \(V_g\) is applied between time instants \(t_0\) and \(t_1\). After \(t_1\), during the MOSFET turn-OFF process, it experiences a voltage overshoot. [figure unavailable] Based on the \(V_{ds}\) waveforms shown in Figure (b), which one of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation:
From \(t=0\) to \(t=t_1\), during the turn-ON condition of the MOSFET, current flows through the inductor, and the inductor charges. After \(t_1\), during the MOSFET turn-OFF process, the inductor tries to discharge through the diode (\(D\)) and the resistor (\(R_f\)). [figure unavailable] Assuming the diode is ideal, the voltage across the inductor can be written as \[V_L = i_L R_f\] where the discharging current is given by \[i_L = I_o e^{-t/\tau}\] Using KVL, the voltage across the MOSFET during the turn-OFF condition (\(V_{ds}\)) can be calculated as \[V_{ds} = V_{DC} + V_L\] \[V_{ds} = V_{DC} + i_L R_f\] As the resistance \(R_f\) increases, the peak voltage across the MOSFET \(V_{ds}\) increases. Based on the given relationship and circuit behavior, \[\boxed{B}\]
Key points
  • During turn-off of a switch in an inductive circuit, the stored energy in the inductor causes a voltage spike (\(L \frac{di}{dt}\)).
  • The peak voltage across the switch is the sum of the supply voltage and the transient voltage across the discharge resistor.
  • The time constant \(\tau = \frac{L}{R}\) dictates the rate of discharge; a higher resistance leads to a faster discharge but a higher peak voltage.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Neglecting the polarity of \(V_L\) during discharging; it adds to \(V_{DC}\) across the switch.
  • Forgetting that \(V_{ds}\) reaches its maximum value at the instant of turn-off when \(i_L\) is maximum.

questions.ref: AC to DC Converters/Phase Controlled Rectifiers Q1
questions.question: Consider the circuit shown. Assume that the diode \(D\) is ideal. The supply voltage is \(v_s = 325 \sin(2\pi \cdot 50t)\,\text{V}\), with \(L = 500\,\mu\text{H}\) and \(R = 10\,\Omega\). The peak diode current (in amperes) is (Round off to one decimal place.) questions.explanation: \[R = 10\,\Omega, \quad L = 500\,\mu\text{F}\] First, calculating the inductive reactance (\(X_{L}\)) at a standard power frequency of \(f = 50\,\text{Hz}\): \[X_{L} = \omega L = 2\pi \cdot 50 \cdot 500 \cdot 10^{-6}\] \[X_{L} = 0.157\,\Omega\] The total magnitude of the load impedance (\(|Z|\)) is given by: \[|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + X_{L}^2} = \sqrt{10^2 + (0.157)^2} = 10.001\,\Omega \simeq R\] Since the inductive reactance value is extremely small compared to the resistance (\(X_{L} \ll R\)), the total impedance magnitude is dominated entirely by the resistor: \[|Z| \simeq R\] Therefore, we can approximate the network as a pure load resistance. Given \(v_s = 100 \sin(2\pi 50t)\ \text{V}\), \(V_{dc} = 50\ \text{V}\), and \(R = 10\ \Omega\), the average value of the current through the diode is \(\text{A}\) (round off to two decimal places) [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Method 1
The transient current equation When the supply voltage \(V_{s}\) exceeds \(50\,\text{V}\), the conduction starts. \[i = \frac{V_{s} - 50}{10} = 10\sin\alpha - 5\] Conduction occurs between the conduction angles where \(i > 0\). Equating \(i = 0\) \[10\sin\alpha = 5 \implies \sin\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\] This yields the lower limit \(\alpha = \frac{\pi}{6}\) and the upper limit \(\alpha = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}\). [figure unavailable] Average current (\(I_{\text{avg}}\))
\[I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6} i \cdot d\alpha\] \[I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6} (10\sin\alpha - 5)\,d\alpha\] \[I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \Big[ -10\cos\alpha - 5\alpha \Big]_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\] \[I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{-1}{2\pi} \left\{ \left[ 10\cos\frac{5\pi}{6} - 10\cos\frac{\pi}{6} \right] + \left[ 5\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) - 5\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \right] \right\}\] \[I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \left[ 17.32 - 10.47 \right] = \frac{6.85}{2\pi} \approx 1.08\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{1.08}\]
Method 2
[figure unavailable] Calculation of Conduction Angles The conduction begins when the instantaneous supply voltage reaches the battery voltage level \(E\): \[\theta_{1} = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{E}{V_{m}}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{50}{100}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6} \quad (30^{\circ})\] Due to the symmetry of the sine wave, the conduction stops when the supply falls back below \(E\): \[\theta_{2} = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6} \quad (150^{\circ})\] Integration for Average Current The average current equation over a full cycle (\(2\pi\)) is given by: \[I_{D} = I_{0} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \cdot \int_{\theta_{1}}^{\theta_{2}} \left( \frac{V_{m}\sin\omega t - E}{R} \right) d(\omega t)\] \[= \frac{1}{2\pi \cdot 10} \cdot \left[ 100(\cos 30^{\circ} - \cos 150^{\circ}) - 50\left(\frac{5\pi}{6} - \frac{\pi}{6}\right) \right]\] \[= \frac{1}{20\pi} \cdot \left[ 100\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right) - 50\left(\frac{4\pi}{6}\right) \right]\] \[= \frac{1}{20\pi} \cdot \left[ 100\sqrt{3} - \frac{100\pi}{3} \right]\] \[= \frac{1}{20\pi} \cdot \left[ 173.20 - 104.72 \right] = \frac{68.48}{20\pi} \approx 1.08\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{1.08}\]

questions.question: Consider the boost converter circuit shown. Assume that the semiconductor devices are ideal. In steady state, the inductor current rises linearly from \(0\ \text{A}\) to \(6\ \text{A}\) in the first \(10\,\mu\text{s}\) and then falls linearly from \(6\ \text{A}\) to \(0\ \text{A}\) in the next \(10\,\mu\text{s}\) of every switching cycle as shown. The load resistance \(R\) is \(10\ \Omega\) and the capacitance \(C\) is \(500\,\mu\text{F}\). [figure unavailable] Neglect the ripple in the output voltage. What is the input voltage \(V_{dc}\)?
questions.explanation:
Given that the inductor current rises for \(10\,\mu\text{s}\) and falls for \(10\,\mu\text{s}\) over a complete switching cycle, the duty cycle (\(D\)) of the converter is calculated as: \[D = \frac{T_{\text{on}}}{T_{\text{on}} + T_{\text{off}}} = \frac{10\,\mu\text{s}}{10\,\mu\text{s} + 10\,\mu\text{s}} = 0.5\] For an ideal boost converter operating in continuous conduction mode (CCM), the relationship between input voltage (\(V_{\text{in}}\)) and output voltage (\(V_{\text{out}}\)) is expressed as: \[V_{\text{out}} = \frac{V_{\text{in}}}{1 - D} = \frac{V_{\text{in}}}{1 - 0.5} = 2V_{\text{in}}\] Average inductor current is \(3\,\text{A}\) \[I_{\text{out}} = \frac{V_{\text{out}}}{10}\] Applying the input-to-output power balance equation (\(P_{\text{in}} = P_{\text{out}}\)) for an ideal lossless converter: \[V_{\text{in}} \times I_{\text{L(avg)}} = \frac{V_{\text{out}}^{2}}{10}\] Substituting \(I_{\text{L(avg)}} = 3\,\text{A}\) and \(V_{\text{out}} = 2V_{\text{in}}\) into the power balance equation: \[V_{\text{in}} \times 3 = \frac{(2V_{\text{in}})^{2}}{10}\] \[3V_{\text{in}} = \frac{4V_{\text{in}}^{2}}{10}\] Assuming \(V_{\text{in}} \neq 0\), we can divide both sides by \(V_{\text{in}}\): \[3 = \frac{4V_{\text{in}}}{10}\] \[4V_{\text{in}} = 30 \implies V_{\text{in}} = 7.5\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{7.5}\]
Key points
  • Boost Converter Voltage Ratio: In critical conduction mode, a boost converter steps up voltage according to the conversion ratio \(V_{\text{out}} = \frac{V_{\text{in}}}{1-D}\).
  • Power Conservation Principle: For any ideal DC-DC converter, average input power equals average output power (\(V_{\text{in}}I_{\text{in}} = V_{\text{out}}I_{\text{out}}\)).

questions.question: Exacerbate : Mitigate :: ________ Choose the option with the correct pair of words to fill the blank.
questions.explanation:
We need to find the word pair whose relationship mirrors the baseline analogy *Exacerbate : Mitigate*. Let us define the core semantic relationship linking these two verbs:
  • Exacerbate: To make a problem worse, more severe, or to intensify a negative state.
  • Mitigate: To make a problem less severe, serious, or to alleviate a negative state.
The baseline relationship follows an **antonym pair** structure where both words operate along the same scalar dimension (the severity or intensity of a problem). We evaluate each option against this exact framework:
  • Option A (Aggravate : Alleviate): *Aggravate* means to worsen or intensify a problem (synonymous with *exacerbate*), while *alleviate* means to make a problem less severe or relieve it (synonymous with *mitigate*). This perfectly replicates the antonym relationship along the identical semantic axis.
  • Option B and C: *Precipitate* means to cause something to happen suddenly or prematurely, which fails to track the direct antonym axis of *mitigate*.
  • Option D (Emancipate : Exonerate): Both words carry distinct positive legal meanings (*emancipate* means to set free; *exonerate* means to absolve from blame), meaning they are not antonyms.
Therefore, Option A is the uniquely correct parallel pair. \[\boxed{\text{A. Aggravate : Alleviate}}\]
Key points
  • The relationship is a parallel matching antonym set: \(\text{Exacerbate} \approx \text{Aggravate}\) and \(\text{Mitigate} \approx \text{Alleviate}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Avoid selecting pairs based solely on generic positive or negative connotations; the target choice must mirror the precise action-oriented antonym axis of the prompt.

questions.question: Four people P, Q, R, and S, of different ages, make the following observations. P -- I am younger than S. Q -- I am neither the youngest nor the oldest. R -- P is older than me. Based on these observations, the youngest person is _____.
questions.explanation:
From the given logical statements, we need to determine who is the youngest individual among P, Q, R, and S. We break down the relational constraints and inequalities from each statement (where higher value indicates older age):
  1. P's Statement: \(P < S\) (P is younger than S).
  2. R's Statement: \(R < P\) (R is younger than P).
  3. Chaining the Inequalities: Combining these two structural relations gives the ordering chain: \[R < P < S\]
  4. Q's Statement: Q states that he is neither the youngest (\(\min\)) nor the oldest (\(\max\)).
Let us analyze where Q can be placed within the established chain \(R < P < S\). Since Q cannot be the absolute youngest or oldest, Q cannot be placed to the left of R or to the right of S. Q must fit somewhere within the internal bounds of the sequence, meaning \(R < Q\) and \(Q < S\). Regardless of whether Q is older or younger than P, R remains bounded at the absolute minimum position of the ordering chain under all valid permutations. Therefore, R is strictly the youngest individual. This logical derivation matches Option C. \[\boxed{\text{C. R}}\]
Key points
  • Chaining linear inequalities allows you to establish definitive minimum and maximum boundary elements across a dataset.
  • Boundary constraints like ``neither min nor max'' eliminate items from extreme positions without needing to fix their exact internal rank.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not waste time trying to find the exact relative age rank between P and Q; their internal positioning has no mathematical effect on identifying the absolute minimum boundary element.

questions.question: ``He often _______ the numbers. False claims are not going to help. Honesty _______ trust'', said the manager. Choose the option with the correct order of words to fill the blanks.
questions.explanation:
We need to determine the correct pair of words to logically complete the manager's statement regarding transparency and corporate metrics. An analysis of the first sentence segment, ``He often the numbers. False claims are not going to help,'' indicates that the individual alters or inflates numeric values, as established by the negative context of ``false claims.'' The verb exaggerates fits this meaning directly. Looking at the second sentence segment, ``Honesty trust,'' the statement expresses a foundational principle where being honest acts as a structural catalyst that creates or gives rise to trust. The verb engenders means precisely to cause, produce, or give rise to a feeling or situation. Evaluating the alternatives:
  • Option A (exaggerates; engenders): Fits both contextual positions perfectly.
  • Option B (excels; encourages): The phrase ``excels the numbers'' is grammatically incorrect.
  • Option C (aggravates; alleviates): ``Aggravates the numbers'' does not fit the semantic context.
  • Option D (diminishes; eliminates): Contradicts the sentence logic because honesty does not eliminate trust.
Hence, Option A is the uniquely consistent choice. \[\boxed{\text{A. exaggerates; engenders}}\]
Key points
  • Exaggerate means to represent something as being larger, greater, or better than it really is.
  • Engender is a precise verb signifying to cause or breed a specific systemic condition.

questions.explanation:
We need to find the pair of words \((P, Q)\) that satisfies the double analogy relation: \[\text{Charity} : P :: \text{Retaliation} : Q\] Establishing the core semantic relationships links a specific human behavior to its motivating character trait. Charity is an action driven by someone who is defined as magnanimous (generous, kind, and forgiving). Parallel to this, retaliation is an action driven by someone who is defined as vindictive (vengeful, spiteful, and seeking revenge). Testing the alternatives shows that Option A is incorrect because *parsimonious* means stingy, which is the opposite of charity. Option B is incorrect because *amicable* means friendly, which contradicts retaliation. Option C is incorrect because *resentful* is a temporary emotion rather than a character trait that matches the structural setup. Therefore, **Option D** (\(P = \text{Magnanimous}; \ Q = \text{Vindictive}\)) is the only pair that completes the parallel analogy layout. \[\boxed{\text{D. P = Magnanimous; Q = Vindictive}}\]
Key points
  • The analogy maps an action to its defining character trait: \(\text{[Action]} : \text{[Adjective describing the actor]}\).

questions.explanation:
We need to find the antonym of the word protagonist. A protagonist is defined as the leading character, hero, or principal figure in a novel, play, or story. Conversely, an antagonist is a person who actively opposes or is hostile to someone or something; in literature, it represents the principal adversary of the protagonist. Evaluating the remaining options:
  • Aagnostic: A person who believes that nothing is known or can be known of the existence or nature of God.
  • Carsonist: A person who deliberately sets fire to property.
  • Danarchist: A person who rebels against any authority, established order, or ruling power.
Hence, Option B is the direct antonym. \[\boxed{\text{B. antagonist}}\]
Key points
  • Protagonist (Greek prōtagōnistēs: first actor) and Antagonist (Greek antagōnistēs: competitor/opponent) form a classic literary antonym pair based on opposing Greek prefixes.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: `When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently.' If the above statement is true, which one of the following statements is not necessarily true?
options: If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent.
If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing.
questions.explanation:
Given the true conditional premise: ``When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently,'' we need to identify which statement is not necessarily true. Let us express the prompt statement in standard propositional logic notation: * Let \(P\) = The teacher is in the room. * Let \(Q\) = All students stand silently. The premise states that \(P \implies Q\) is **True**. Let us analyze the logical validity of each option:
  • Option A: ``If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room.'' This translates to \( eg Q \implies eg P\), which is the **contrapositive** of our premise. A contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original implication statement, so this is strictly True.
  • Option B: ``When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent.'' This is a restatement of \(P \implies Q\), which is explicitly True.
  • Option C: ``If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.'' This translates to \(Q \implies P\), which is the **converse** of our premise. The truth of an implication does not guarantee the truth of its converse (affirming the consequent). Thus, this is not necessarily true.
  • Option D: ``When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing.'' This is a valid direct restatement of the conditional premise, so it is strictly True.
Hence, Option C is not necessarily true. \[ oxed{ ext{ C. If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.}}\]
Key points
  • Given a true implication \(P \implies Q\), its contrapositive (\( eg Q \implies eg P\)) is guaranteed to be true, while its converse (\(Q \implies P\)) and inverse (\( eg P \implies eg Q\)) are logical fallacies and not necessarily true.

questions.question:
Combinatorics deals with problems involving counting. For example, ``How many distinct arrangements of N distinct objects in M spaces on a circle are possible?'' is a typical problem in combinatorics. This kind of counting is sometimes used in the modeling of several physical phenomena. Often, in such models, the different combinatorial possibilities are assigned probability values. Assigning probabilities enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities. Consider the following statements:
  • P: Combinatorics is always invoked in the modeling of physical phenomena.
  • Q: Modeling some physical phenomena involves assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities in order to compute average values of physical quantities.
Based on the passage above, what can be inferred about statements P and Q?
options: P is False and Q is False
P is False and Q is True
P is True and Q is False
P is True and Q is True
questions.explanation:
Based on the text passage regarding combinatorics and physical modeling, we need to determine the truth values of statements P and Q. Let us analyze the text to evaluate each statement:
  • Statement P: ``Combinatorics is always invoked in the modeling of physical phenomena.'' The text states that combinatorics is ``sometimes used in the modeling of several physical phenomena.'' The absolute qualifier **always** in statement P overextends this claim, making statement P **False**.
  • Statement Q: ``Modeling some physical phenomena involves assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities in order to compute average values of physical quantities.'' The text explicitly notes: ``Often, in such models, the different combinatorial possibilities are assigned probability values. Assigning probabilities enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities.'' This matches statement Q directly, making it **True**.
Therefore, P is False and Q is True, which corresponds to Option B. \[\boxed{\text{ B. P is False and Q is True}}\]
Key points
  • Critical reading requires distinguishing between absolute constraints (e.g., *always*, *must*) and partial conditions (e.g., *sometimes*, *often*) mentioned in text passages.

Accelerate also means to cause something to move faster or happen sooner, matching the synonym series perfectly. The remaining choices are contextually incorrect: Retard means to delay or slow down, Provide means to supply or make available, and Disable means to incapacitate. \[\boxed{\text{A. Accelerate}}\]
Key points

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: `When it is raining, peacocks dance.' Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?
options: Peacocks dance only when it is raining.
When peacocks dance, it is raining.
When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.
When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.
questions.explanation:
Given the conditional premise statement: ``When it is raining, peacocks dance,'' we need to identify which statement is necessarily true. Let us express the premise statement using propositional logic operators: * Let \(R\) = It is raining. * Let \(D\) = Peacocks dance. The prompt statement means that the implication \(R \implies D\) is **True**. Let us analyze the logical validity of the choices:
  • Choice A: ``Peacocks dance only when it is raining.'' This maps to \(D \implies R\) (the converse), which is a logical fallacy and not necessarily true.
  • Choice B: ``When peacocks dance, it is raining.'' This is another restatement of the converse \(D \implies R\), which is not necessarily true.
  • Choice C: ``When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.'' This translates directly to \( eg D \implies eg R\), which is the **contrapositive** of our premise. Since a conditional statement and its contrapositive are always logically equivalent, this statement is strictly True.
  • Choice D: ``When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.'' This maps to \( eg R \implies eg D\) (the inverse), which is not necessarily true.
\[ oxed{ ext{C. When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.}}\]
Key points
  • For any fundamentally true implication \(P \implies Q\), its conditional contrapositive (\( eg Q \implies eg P\)) is always logically guaranteed to be true.

questions.question: Water : P :: Food : Q Choose the P and Q combination from the options below to form a meaningful analogy.
questions.explanation:
We need to find a combination for \((P, Q)\) that completes the double analogy: \(\text{Water} : P :: \text{Food} : Q\). Let us analyze the biological relationship linking each substance to its matching physiological sensation:
  • Water is consumed to relieve the physical sensation of Thirst.
  • Food is consumed to relieve the physical sensation of Hunger.
This establishes a parallel relationship, where each substance acts as the direct counter-agent to satisfy a specific physiological need. Setting \(P = \text{Thirst}\) and \(Q = \text{Hunger}\) creates a perfectly balanced double analogy along identical biological axes. \[\boxed{\text{A. P = Thirst; Q = Hunger}}\]
Key points
  • Analogy structures require maintaining an identical relationship axis (Substance : Corresponding Deprivation Sensation) across both comparison pairs.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: `The shopkeeper sells lemons.' In this sentence, the word `lemons' is the ________.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify the grammatical function of the word `lemons' in the sentence: ``The shopkeeper sells lemons.'' Let us break down the functional parts of the clause:
  • Subject: ``The shopkeeper'' (the agent performing the action).
  • Verb: ``sells'' (the action being performed).
  • Object: ``lemons'' (the entity receiving the direct action of the verb).
This matches A. \[\boxed{\text{A. object}}\]
Key points
  • A direct object is a noun or pronoun that directly receives the action of a transitive verb, answering the question what? or whom?.

questions.question: `If Anish had scored hundred runs in today's match, he would have been made the captain of his team. He would have then become the youngest captain in his team's history. Unfortunately, he got out without scoring any runs. Hence, there won't be any change in the captaincy for now.' Based on the paragraph above, which one of the following statements is true?
options: Anish made hundred runs but was denied captaincy.
Anish was the captain of his team before the game today.
The current captain is older than Anish.
Anish is the youngest player in his team.
questions.explanation:
Based on the provided biographical text segment regarding team selection criteria, we evaluate the statements to identify which claim is strictly true. Let us cross-examine each option against the facts established in the paragraph:
  • The text presents a conditional scenario: *If* Anish had scored a century, he *would* have become the captain and been the youngest captain in history.
  • However, the text explicitly reveals what actually happened: ``Unfortunately, he got out without scoring any runs. Hence, there won't be any change in the captaincy for now.''
  • This confirms that the current captain remains in office, and because Anish would have broken a history record as the youngest candidate had he succeeded, it logically follows that the current, un-displaced captain must be older than him.
This matches statement C. \[\boxed{\text{C. The current captain is older than Anish.}}\]
Key points
  • Subjunctive conditional statements (e.g., ``If he had...'') describe hypothetical scenarios; factual tracking must rely on the direct, unconditional assertions in the text.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: `The team _____ more than 300 runs in 20 overs _______ rains. However, some players needed to improve their batting skills.' Choose the option with the correct sequence of words to fill the blanks.
questions.explanation:
We need to choose the correct sequence of words to fill the blanks in the sentence: ``The team more than 300 runs in 20 overs rains.'' Let us analyze each clause contextually:
  • First Blank: The sentence concludes with a descriptive statement in the past tense (``some players needed to improve...''). Therefore, the initial independent clause must be in the simple past tense to maintain narrative consistency. This isolates scored.
  • Second Blank: The sentence introduces a counter-premise (rains). The preposition despite means ``notwithstanding'' or ``in spite of'' and perfectly transitions a noun phrase without a helping verb.
This corresponds to C. \[\boxed{\text{C. scored; despite}}\]
Key points
  • Prepositions like despite or in spite of function to introduce a contrastive noun phrase, whereas conjunctions like although require a complete subordinate clause.
